body.objective: Students will be able to read dotted rhythms.
successCriteria: I can count and perform dotted rhythms
I can explain what a dot does to a note
I can recognize dotted rhythms in songs
body.hook: Have you ever noticed that some songs make you want to move more than others? Often it's because of rhythms that don't land right on the beat. A dot after a note, or an accent in an unexpected place, can turn a plain rhythm into something with groove.

vocabulary.definition: A symbol after a note that adds half the note's value.
A note worth 3 beats in 4/4 time.
A note worth 1½ beats in 4/4 time, often followed by an eighth note.
A curved line joining two notes of the same pitch so they are held as one.
Counting smaller parts of the beat, such as "1-and-2-and."
The feel of a rhythm that makes people want to move.

study.title: Connect the Dots
study.question: How does a dot change rhythm?
study.passage:
The dot rule: a dot adds half the value of the note.
• Half note (2) + dot (1) = dotted half note = 3 beats
• Quarter note (1) + dot (½) = dotted quarter note = 1½ beats
A dotted quarter note is usually followed by an eighth note so the pair fills 2 beats: count "1 (2) and."
Part 1, Subdivide (5 minutes): Count "1-and-2-and-3-and-4-and" aloud while tapping the beat.
Part 2, Tie to dot (10 minutes): Clap a quarter note tied to an eighth note, then see that it sounds exactly like a dotted quarter. Write both versions on the board.
Part 3, Rhythm reading (10 minutes), all in 4/4:
Line 1: dotted half, quarter
Line 2: dotted quarter, eighth, half
Line 3: quarter, dotted quarter, eighth, quarter
Line 4: dotted quarter, eighth, dotted quarter, eighth
Part 4, Listen (5 minutes): Many familiar tunes use a dotted quarter and eighth near the start. Sing or play "Auld Lang Syne" (public domain): the words "auld ac-" (in "auld acquaintance") use a dotted quarter and an eighth.
Part 5, Perform (10 minutes): In groups, perform Lines 1–4 as a round on hand drums or body percussion, keeping a steady beat with a metronome at 80 beats per minute.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; "Auld Lang Syne" is a traditional song in the public domain.

body.objective: Students will be able to perform syncopation.
successCriteria: I can count and clap syncopated rhythms
I can hear syncopation in songs
body.hook: Listen to almost any funk, reggae or pop song and you'll notice the accents land in unexpected places, between the beats instead of on them. That off-beat surprise is syncopation, and it's what makes music groove.

vocabulary.definition: Accenting a weak beat or an off-beat instead of the strong beat.
Extra emphasis on a note, shown by the symbol >.
A curved line joining two notes of the same pitch into one longer sound.
A beat that is naturally stressed, such as beat 1 in 4/4.
A rhythmic feel that makes people want to move.

study.title: Off the Beat
study.question: How does syncopation make rhythm exciting?
study.passage:
Activities (written for this lesson):
1. On-beat vs off-beat (5 minutes): Step on every beat while clapping only the "ands": 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &.
2. The classic syncopation (10 minutes): eighth, quarter, eighth: count "1 & (2) & ". The quarter note starts on the "and" of 1 and carries over beat 2, so the strong beat is skipped. Clap it eight times, then over a steady stomp.
3. Ties (5 minutes): Two eighth notes tied across a beat sound as one note that crosses the beat.
4. Accents (5 minutes): Clap eight steady eighth notes, accenting 1, the "and" of 2, and 4 (>): this is a common Latin and pop pattern.
5. Listening (10 minutes): Clap along to the hook of a popular song with a syncopated rhythm, and to Scott Joplin's "The Entertainer" (1902), a ragtime piece where the right hand is syncopated over a steady left hand.
6. Create (5 minutes): Write one bar that uses syncopation and clap it over a partner's steady beat.

body.objective: Students will be able to follow tempo markings.
successCriteria: I can name and explain common tempo markings
I can use a metronome to perform at a set tempo
I can explain how tempo changes mood
body.hook: The same melody played slowly at a funeral and quickly at a celebration feels completely different. Composers write tempo markings, mostly in Italian, so performers know exactly how fast to go.

vocabulary.definition: Beats per minute; the number of beats in one minute.
A device that clicks a steady beat at a chosen tempo.

study.title: How Fast?
study.question: How do tempo markings shape music?
study.passage:
Tempo guide (written for this lesson; BPM ranges are approximate):
Largo: very slow and broad (about 40–60 BPM).
Adagio: slow (about 66–76).
Andante: walking pace (about 76–108).
Moderato: moderate (about 108–120).
Allegro: fast (about 120–160).
Presto: very fast (about 168–200).
Changes: accelerando (accel.), getting faster; ritardando (rit.), getting slower; a tempo, return to the original speed.
Activities: 1. Walk around the room to a metronome at 60, 90, 120 and 160 BPM; name each tempo. 2. Clap a dotted rhythm at andante, then at allegro. 3. Listen to two excerpts, such as Samuel Barber's Adagio for Strings (1936) and Rossini's William Tell Overture finale (1829); estimate BPM and name the tempo. 4. Perform "Happy Birthday" at largo, then presto. How does the mood change?
